biodiversity-s1.title: Species on rocky-shore plots after a predator is removed
biodiversity-s1.text: On a rocky shore, a predatory sea star eats mussels, barnacles and snails. Researchers marked ten 4 m² plots. From five plots they removed every sea star each month for six years; five control plots were left alone. Each year they counted the species of attached animals and seaweeds in each plot. Sea stars made up less than 1% of the animals counted. Mussels covered about 20% of the rock in every plot at the start; after six years they covered 85% of the removal plots and 15-25% of the control plots. Points are means of five plots.

biodiversity-s2.title: Grassland plots with different numbers of plant species in a drought
biodiversity-s2.text: Ecologists sowed 1 m² plots with 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 grassland plant species, choosing the species for each plot at random from a pool of 18, with 30 plots of each kind. They measured the plant matter (biomass) above ground each summer. One summer brought a severe drought. Values are means ± 2 SE.

table.caption: Biomass before, during and after the drought
cols: Biomass the summer before the drought (g per m²)
Biomass lost in the drought (% of the summer before)
Biomass two years later (% of the summer before)

items.q: Which statement best describes the results?
options: Species numbers fell in both kinds of plot, but more slowly in the control plots than in the removal plots.
The control plots stayed at 15-16 species, while removal plots fell steadily from 15 to 7 species over six years.
Removal plots lost most of their species in the first year and then held steady at about 14 species per plot after that.
Removal plots gained species as the mussels spread, rising above the control plots by year 6.

why.correct: Control plots held 15-16 species throughout; removal plots dropped each year: 15, 14, 12, 10, 9, 8, 7.
options: The control plots did not decline; they varied between 15 and 16.
Correct: a steady fall only where the sea stars were removed.
The removal plots lost 1 species in year 1 and kept declining to 7.
Removal plots lost species as mussels spread, ending at 7 against 15 in the controls.

items.q: By what percentage did the number of species in the removal plots fall from year 0 to year 6? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Which explanation best accounts for the loss of species from the removal plots?
options: Without sea stars eating them, mussels spread over the rock and crowded out species that need space to attach.
Without sea stars, the snails and barnacles they ate became too numerous and starved, taking other species with them.
Removing the sea stars disturbed the rock surface each month, which killed many of the attached species.
Sea stars release nutrients in their wastes, and without them the seaweeds and animals had too little food.

why.correct: The sea star keeps mussels, the strongest competitor for space, in check. Mussel cover rose from 20% to 85%, and the species that lost their space disappeared: competitive exclusion released by removing the predator.
options: Correct: the predator held down the dominant competitor.
The data show mussels taking over the rock, not prey starving.
Removing sea stars by hand is a small disturbance; the steady rise in mussel cover explains the losses better.
Nothing in the data points to nutrients, and the loss tracks the spread of mussels.

items.q: Which claim about the sea star is best supported by the data?
options: It is a foundation species, because the community is built on its large numbers.
It is a keystone species, because a scarce species had a large effect on the community.
It is an ecosystem engineer, because it changes the physical structure of the rock it lives on.
It is a competitor of the mussels, because both use space on the rock.

why.correct: Sea stars were under 1% of the animals counted, yet removing them cut species numbers by more than half: an effect far larger than their abundance, the mark of a keystone species.
options: Foundation species are abundant; the sea star is scarce.
Correct: a small share of the community with a large effect.
The sea star acts by eating mussels, not by building or reshaping the habitat.
The sea star eats mussels; it is their predator, not a competitor for space.

items.q: In a second experiment, researchers instead removed one rare red seaweed from five plots for six years. Predict the result.
options: Species numbers fall to about 7, as in the sea star removal plots.
Species numbers rise, because the seaweed was a strong competitor for space.
Mussels spread over 85% of the rock, because they lose a food source.
Species numbers stay near the control level, apart from the lost seaweed.

why.correct: A rare species without a key role leaves little gap; its loss lowers richness by about one, while the mussels are still held down by the sea stars.
options: The steep loss came from releasing the dominant competitor; a rare seaweed does not hold mussels back.
A rare species is unlikely to be a strong competitor, so removing it frees little space.
Mussels filter food from the water; a rare seaweed is not their food, and sea stars still eat them.
Correct: losing a non-keystone species has a small effect.

items.q: Which statement best describes the relationship shown in the table?
options: Plots with more species produced less biomass but lost a larger share in the drought.
Plots with more species lost a smaller share in the drought but were slower to return to their earlier biomass.
Plots with more species produced more biomass, lost a smaller share in the drought and recovered more fully.
Plots with different numbers of species lost similar shares of their biomass in the drought.

why.correct: From 1 to 16 species, biomass rose (180 to 380 g per m²), drought loss fell (78% to 33%) and recovery after two years rose (62% to 101%).
options: Both trends are reversed: more species meant more biomass and a smaller loss.
Recovery was more complete with more species (101% vs 62%).
Correct: higher productivity, resistance and resilience with more species.
Losses ranged from 78% to 33%, a large difference.

items.q: Using the means, calculate the biomass left in the 16-species plots during the drought, in g per m². Give a whole number.

why.correct: They lost 33% of 380 g per m², keeping 67%: 0.67 × 380 = 254.6, about 255 g per m². (The 1-species plots kept 0.22 × 180 ≈ 40 g per m².)

items.q: Using the error bars (± 2 SE), which conclusion about drought losses is best supported?
options: 8-species and 16-species plots differ clearly, because their means differ by 8 percentage points.
1-species and 16-species plots do not clearly differ, because both sets of error bars are large.
1-species and 16-species plots differ clearly, but 8-species and 16-species plots do not clearly differ.
No two kinds of plot clearly differ, because each mean has an error bar around it.

why.correct: 1 species: 68-88%; 16 species: 27-39%. No overlap, so they clearly differ. 8 species: 34-48% overlaps 27-39%, so those two are not clearly different.
options: The intervals 34-48% and 27-39% overlap, so this difference may be due to chance.
The intervals 68-88% and 27-39% are far apart.
Correct: compare the ± 2 SE intervals for overlap.
Error bars that do not overlap, such as those for 1 and 16 species, indicate a clear difference.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the smaller drought losses in plots with many species?
options: Plants in diverse plots shade the soil so well that drought does not reach their roots.
Diverse plots are more likely to include drought-tolerant species that keep growing and use resources the others leave.
Each species in a diverse plot grows more slowly, so each needs less water during a drought.
Diverse plots were watered more often by the researchers to keep the many species alive.

why.correct: Species differ in how they cope with drought. The more species a plot has, the more likely some are deep-rooted or drought-tolerant and can take over, so the plot as a whole loses less and recovers faster.
options: Shading may help a little, but the plots still lost a third of their biomass, so the drought did reach them.
Correct: differences among species buffer the whole community.
Diverse plots produced more biomass, not less, so their plants were not growing more slowly.
The design gave every plot the same treatment; nothing suggests extra watering.

items.q: Why did the researchers choose the species for each plot at random from the pool of 18?
options: So that the effect measured is of species number, not of always including one especially hardy species
So that each plot ends up with exactly the same total number of plants after it is sown
So that the 1-species plots each contain the most drought-tolerant species in the pool
So that the plots with more species are planted in the wettest parts of the field

why.correct: If the 16-species plots always held a particular hardy species, it could be that species, not diversity, that reduced losses. Random draws spread every species across plots of every diversity level.
options: Correct: randomization separates the number of species from the identity of particular species.
Random choice of species does not set plant numbers; that is controlled by how the seeds are sown.
Choosing the hardiest species on purpose would bias the comparison, the opposite of randomizing.
Placing diverse plots in wet spots would confound the result; the species draw does not do that.

items.q: Beavers cut trees and build dams that flood a stream valley, creating a pond with marshy edges where frogs, ducks and water plants live. Which term best describes the beaver's role?
options: Foundation species, because beavers are the most abundant animals there
Producer, because beavers supply the energy that the pond relies on
Keystone predator, because beavers eat the strongest competitor present
Ecosystem engineer, because beavers physically reshape the environment

why.correct: Beavers change the physical environment, turning a stream into a pond and wetland that many other species then use.
options: Beavers are few; their effect comes from building, not from being abundant.
Beavers are consumers; the pond's energy comes from its plants and algae.
Beavers eat bark and plants; their effect is not through predation on a competitor.
Correct: a species that creates habitat by changing the physical environment.

items.q: In a meadow, removing species X (2% of the plant and animal biomass) cut the number of species by half, while removing species Y (40% of the biomass) cut it by 10%. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Y is a keystone species, because it makes up the most biomass in the meadow.
Neither is a keystone species, because removing either one lowered richness.
X is a keystone species, because its effect is far larger than its share of the biomass.
Both are keystone species, because removing either one of them changed the whole community.

why.correct: Keystone species are identified by an effect out of proportion to abundance: X, at 2% of biomass, halved richness.
options: A species that is abundant and has a modest effect fits a dominant species, not a keystone.
Lowering richness does not rule out a keystone role; X's effect is huge for its size.
Correct: small share, large effect.
Nearly any removal changes a community a little; Y's effect is in line with its large share.

items.q: On a savanna, elephants push over and eat young trees, which keeps the land open and grassy. Zebras and wildebeest graze the grass. All elephants are removed from a large fenced reserve. Predict each quantity ten years later.

variables.name: Number of trees
variables.why: Young trees are no longer pushed over and eaten, so more of them grow up.

variables.name: Area of open grassland
variables.why: Growing trees shade out grass and take over space that was open.

variables.name: Number of grazing zebras and wildebeest
variables.why: Less grass means less food for grazers.

variables.name: Yearly rainfall on the reserve
variables.why: Rainfall is set by regional weather, not by elephants in one reserve.

why.correct: Elephants act as ecosystem engineers, holding back trees. Without them, the savanna moves toward woodland, and the species that depend on open grassland decline.

items.q: Select the two examples of ecosystem services.
options: Wild bees pollinating apple trees in nearby orchards
A factory producing fertilizer from nitrogen gas
A wetland filtering sediment and nutrients from river water
A farmer buying seeds of a new crop variety
A city building a concrete wall along a river

why.correct: Ecosystem services are benefits that natural ecosystems provide to people, such as pollination and water filtration.
options: An ecosystem service: wild pollinators raise crop yields.
A human industrial process, not a service from an ecosystem.
An ecosystem service: wetlands clean water.
A purchase, not a benefit an ecosystem provides.
Built infrastructure; a floodplain wetland doing the same job would be a service.

items.q: A banana variety grown worldwide for decades was propagated by cuttings, so every plant was a clone. A soil fungus spread through plantations and the variety was largely abandoned. Which explanation best accounts for the collapse?
options: Clones grow more slowly than plants from seed, so the fungus overtook them.
Bananas lack an immune system, so no banana plant can resist any fungus.
Cuttings carry the fungus from parent to offspring, so each clone started life infected.
Every plant had the same alleles, so none had a defense against the fungus.

why.correct: With no genetic diversity, a pathogen that can infect one plant can infect them all; a varied population would likely include some resistant plants.
options: Growth rate is not the issue; susceptibility was shared by every plant.
Plants do have defenses, and some banana varieties resist this fungus; this one did not.
Infected cuttings can spread the fungus, but clean plants in infected soil fell ill too; no plant could resist it.
Correct: no genetic variation, no resistant individuals.

items.q: A region contains oak woods, peat bogs, meadows and streams. This variety is an example of
options: genetic diversity
species evenness among habitats
relative abundance
ecosystem diversity

why.correct: Different kinds of ecosystem in a region are ecosystem diversity, the broadest level of biodiversity.
options: Genetic diversity is variety of alleles within a species.
Evenness describes how equally individuals are spread among species.
Relative abundance is one species' share of the individuals in a community.
Correct: a variety of ecosystems.

items.q: Reef P has 30 coral species, and one of them makes up most of the coral cover; its Simpson's D is 0.52. Reef Q has 22 coral species, all about equally common; its D is 0.95. Which claim is best supported?
options: Reef P is more diverse, because it has more species than reef Q.
The reefs are equally diverse, because both have over 20 coral species.
Reef Q is more diverse, because its species are much more evenly represented.
Reef Q is less stable, because a lower number of species means less diversity.

why.correct: D combines richness and evenness. Q's higher D shows that two random corals there are far more likely to be different species, so Q is more diverse despite fewer species.
options: Richness is only part of diversity; P is dominated by one species.
Their D values (0.52 and 0.95) differ widely.
Correct: higher D, higher diversity.
Q has the higher diversity index, which, if anything, suggests greater stability.

items.q: In one forest, three bird species eat the same kinds of insects. In another, one fig species is the only food source for many fruit-eating animals during the dry season. Which loss would most likely change its community more, and why?
options: Losing one insect-eating bird, because birds are higher on the food chain than trees
Losing the fig, because no other species fills its role and many animals rely on it
Losing one insect-eating bird, because insects would then multiply without limit
Losing either one changes its community equally, because each is one species

why.correct: When several species do the same job, the others can take over if one is lost. The fig has no stand-in during the dry season, so its loss affects every animal that depends on it.
options: Position in the food chain does not decide importance; having no stand-in does.
Correct: a unique role makes a species hard to replace.
The other two bird species still eat the same insects, so insects stay in check.
Species differ in how replaceable they are; losses are not equal.

items.q: A summer of unusually warm water kills most of the reef-building corals on a reef. The heat itself does not harm the reef fish. Predict what happens to the reef fish over the next few years.
options: Fish species decline, because the coral structure they shelter and feed in breaks down.
Fish species increase, because the corals no longer compete with the fish for food.
Fish species stay the same, because the warm water did not harm the fish themselves.
Fish species decline at first and then recover fully within one year as the coral regrows.

why.correct: Reef-building corals are foundation species: their structure is the habitat many fish shelter, feed and breed in. As dead coral erodes, those fish lose their habitat and decline.
options: Correct: losing a foundation species removes the habitat others need.
Corals and reef fish largely use different food; the corals' main effect is to provide habitat.
The fish depend on the coral habitat, so they are affected even though the heat did not harm them.
Reef-building corals grow slowly; recovery takes many years, not one.

items.q: Two lakes lose most of their fish in the same severe winter. Lake A, with 12 fish species, regains its earlier fish biomass in two years; lake B, with 3 species, takes seven years. Lake A shows greater
options: resilience, because it recovered from the disruption faster
species evenness, because its fish biomass returned to normal
carrying capacity, because it supports more species of fish
trophic efficiency, because its fish grew faster after winter

why.correct: Resilience is the speed and completeness of recovery after a disruption; lake A recovered in two years against seven.
options: Correct: faster recovery is resilience.
Evenness describes how equally species are represented, not recovery.
Carrying capacity is for one population; the data are about recovery time.
Trophic efficiency is energy passed between levels; the data do not measure it.

items.q: How does a keystone species differ from a foundation species?
options: A keystone species has an effect far greater than its numbers; a foundation species matters through its abundance and habitat building.
A keystone species is a producer at the base of the food web; a foundation species is a top predator that controls the others.
A keystone species makes up most of the biomass in its community; a foundation species is rare but influential in its effects.
A keystone species changes the physical environment; a foundation species affects others mainly by being eaten by them.

why.correct: Keystone species are defined by an outsized effect relative to abundance, often as predators; foundation species are abundant and build the habitat.
options: Correct: effect relative to abundance versus abundance and habitat.
Keystone species are often predators, and foundation species are often producers such as kelp or trees.
This swaps the two: foundation species are the abundant ones.
Changing the physical environment defines an ecosystem engineer; foundation species matter as habitat, not just as food.

items.q: Which list gives the three levels of biodiversity?
options: Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity
Producers, consumers, decomposers and detritus
Richness, evenness and Simpson's index
Population, community and ecosystem

why.correct: Biodiversity covers the variety of alleles within species, of species in communities and of ecosystems in regions.
options: Correct.
These are trophic roles in an ecosystem.
These describe species diversity, one level only.
These are levels of ecological organization, not of biodiversity.
